answer.rationale:
The tempting move is the switch: the low-cost vendor's quote hits the 18% mandate by itself, and memory_c2 says a prior switch cut unit cost sharply with quick onboarding. That memory is the single load-bearing claim behind the highest-consequence option, so it is the one worth spending the verification budget on. What the consolidated line omits is exactly what matters here: whether that prior switch involved a constrained, line-critical component or a peripheral one, whether it happened with 14 days of runway, and whether the line was at 94% of committed volume with no buffer at the time. 'Onboarding was quick and invoicing stayed accurate' is administrative evidence, not delivery-reliability evidence under load; it says nothing about qualification, first-article yield, or ramp. If the archived record shows a low-stakes part with slack in the schedule, the memory does not transfer to this decision at all.

Absent that confirmation, I intend to negotiate terms at renewal. Memory_c4 shows benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and memory_c6 shows a multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope; combining a benchmarked price challenge with term length is a credible path toward the mandate. Memory_c1 indicates the incumbent integration is stable, so this path carries no migration work against a 14-day cliff and a line with zero buffer. It also keeps the low-cost quote alive as leverage rather than spending it as a commitment.

Risks I am holding open rather than resolving: negotiation may close only part of the 18% gap, in which case the shortfall must be escalated to finance rather than absorbed by a rushed switch; a multi-year commitment reduces this year's unit cost but transfers value downstream by locking out the cheaper vendor and reducing future flexibility, so term length should be the shortest that still unlocks volume pricing. Adding a second source (memory_c3) is the right structural answer to single-point-of-failure exposure but does not address the cost mandate and does not fit the one-decision limit this cycle; deferral (memory_c5) is inapplicable because this contract does not auto-renew and lapse means supply interruption. If archive review of memory_c2 shows the prior switch was genuinely comparable in criticality and timeline, I would revisit switching, but likely as a staged qualification with the incumbent extended, not a hard cutover.
